evidence: Ter. Heaut. 105: Errās, sī id crēdis
Cic. Tusc. 1.39: errāre mehercule mālō cum Platōne
terms.comment: “You’re wrong” is errās; badly wrong, longē errāre (Ter. Ad. 65) or tōtā errāre viā (Ter. Eun. 245).

evidence: Plaut. Most. 968: nē ad aliās aedīs perperam dēvēnerīs
Cic. Quinct. 31: seu rēctē seu perperam facere coepērunt
Traupman 409: if I have done anything wrong, I’m sorry, sī quid perperam fēcī, mē paenitet
terms.comment: The opposite of rēctē. Where English says “the wrong house”, Latin puts the mistake in the verb, as Plautus does.

terms.gloss: wrong, untrue (of what is said or believed)
evidence: Cic. Rep. 2.28: falsum est enim … id tōtum
terms.comment: Of a statement or a belief: falsum est, that isn’t true. Of a person, “mistaken” (Sall. J. 85.20, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Ita dīcō, nē ad aliās aedīs perperam dēvēnerīs.
phrases.english: I’m telling you so that you don’t go to the wrong house by mistake.

phrases.latin: Errās, sī id crēdis, et mē ignōrās, Clīnia.
phrases.english: You’re wrong if you believe that, and you don’t know me, Clinia.

phrases.latin: errāre mehercule mālō cum Platōne … quam cum istīs vēra sentīre
phrases.english: I’d rather be wrong with Plato, by Hercules, … than be right with that crowd

sources: Lewis & Short: erro · Lewis & Short: perperus (perperam) · Lewis & Short: fallo (falsus)
